worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-y}{x-{y}^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{1}-1}{1-{1}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{\sqrt{x}-y}{x-{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-y)(\sqrt{x}+y)}{(x-{y}^{2})(\sqrt{x}+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{2}-{y}^{2}}{(x-{y}^{2})(\sqrt{x}+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{x-{y}^{2}}{(x-{y}^{2})(\sqrt{x}+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+y} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}.$
